title: Leveraging Large Language Models for Sentiment Analysis: Multi-Modal Analysis of Decentraland's MANA Token

p.t: The emergence of blockchain-enabled immersive virtual environments-the Metaverse-has catalyzed interest in persistent digital economies where users transact virtual assets through native cryptocurrencies [1,2]. Decentraland represents a paradigmatic case of this convergence, combining virtual reality with decentralized infrastructure to create economic spheres with unique market dynamics [3]. Its native token, MANA, facilitates transactions for virtual goods and land parcels while conferring governance rights through a decentralized autonomous organization (DAO), rendering it ideal for Start Data Prep Preprocess Load RoBERTa Sentiment Inference Temporal Aggregation End St LSTM Input S t = 1 n t s i,t γ i,t Training Evaluation Fine-tuning Evaluation

Investor sentiment from social media constitutes a significant predictor of market behavior, prompting extensive applications of sentiment analysis in financial forecasting [4]. Within Decentraland, Discord serves as the primary communication channel where user discussions may influence MANA price dynamics. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) have enhanced sentiment analysis capabilities, with multi-agent frameworks improving financial classification accuracy [5] and specialized models advancing emotion detection [6]. This study constructs a multi-modal dataset integrating historical price data with Discord-derived sentiment, trading volume, and market capitalization to forecast token returns. We investigate two research questions (RQs): • (RQ1) What are the prevailing sentiment patterns among Decentraland Discord users, and to what extent do these reflect platform dynamics? • (RQ2) How does integrating multi-modal features affect token return prediction accuracy relative to price-only models? Employing a BERT-based architecture for sentiment extraction and LSTM networks for time-series prediction, we evaluate the incremental value of community sentiment for cryptocurrency forecasting. Figure 1 illustrates the LLM-based sentiment analysis pipeline. 1 II. DATA A. Data Collection 1) Numerical Data: Daily OHLCV data for MANA (ERC-20 utility token [7][8][9]) spanning t ∈ [1, T ] where T = 366 days (June 15, 2023-June 14, 2024) comprise open, high, low, close prices (P O t , P H t , P L t , P C t ), trading volume V t , and market capitalization M t (USD), obtained from CoinMarketCap. 2 2) Textual Data: Discord #general channel messages M = {m i } n i=1 (n = 5, 883) were harvested via DiscordChatExporter, 3 yielding timestamps t i , anonymized author IDs α i , content c i , and engagement metrics. Post-filtering invalid entries, n ′ = 5, 513 messages (M ′ ⊂ M) comprised the final corpus.

The typical price τ t = 1 3 (P H t + P L t + P C t ) serves as the daily indicator, smoothing intraday fluctuations following standard technical analysis practice [10]. 2) Return Calculation: Continuous returns r t = ln(τ t+1 /τ t ) = ln(τ t+1 ) -ln(τ t ) stabilize variance and ensure temporal comparability for ERC-20 token markets [11].

A. Sentiment Analysis 1) LLM Selection: We employ the RoBERTa-based classifier cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest 4 from Hugging Face, pretrained on social media corpora for informal text classification [12,13]. 2) Aggregation: Each message i at time t maps to sentiment s i,t ∈ {+1, 0, -1} (positive, neutral, negative) with confidence γ i,t . Daily sentiment aggregates as S t = 1 nt nt i=1 s i,t γ i,t , where n t denotes daily message volume [14]. Discretization thresholds define S t ∈ [-1, -0.1) as negative, [-0.1, 0.1] as neutral, and (0.1, 1] as positive. B. Return Prediction 1) LSTM Architecture: Long Short-Term Memory networks model sequential dependencies {(x t , r t )} T t=1 via gated mechanisms [15][16][17]: where i t , o t denote input and output gates, σ the sigmoid function, and W, b learned parameters. Model specifications: • Baseline: x t = τ t (scalar, typical price only) • Multi-modal: x t = (τ t , V t , M t , S t ) ′ ∈ R Figure 2 presents the dual analysis of community sentiment dynamics and predictive model performance. The bar plot illustrates the distribution of Discord sentiment over the 366-day observation period: 26.94% positive (s i,t = +1), 60.96% neutral (s i,t = 0), and 12.10% negative (s i,t = -1). This predominance of neutral sentiment with a positive skew indicates stable community affect, with daily aggregate scores S t concentrating within [0, 1]. Notably, negative sentiment spikes correlate primarily with user-level technical issues rather than exogenous market events [23,24], suggesting these data reflect platform user experience rather than macroeconomic signals.

The time-series plots compare the baseline LSTM (priceonly feature x t = τ t ) against the multi-modal architecture (x t = (τ t , V t , M t , S t ) ′ ∈ R 4 ). The multi-modal model improves prediction accuracy, reducing MSE from 0.002100 to 0.001528 and MAE from 0.0297 to 0.0241. However, both models exhibit negative R 2 values (baseline: -0.4185; multimodal: -0.0321), indicating limited explanatory power for directional trends. While auxiliary features enhance short-term precision, they inadequately capture broader market dynamics, consistent with [25].

Our study contributes to metaverse and blockchainempowered virtual economy research [4,[26][27][28][29][30][31][32] and the literature on user-generated content and community sentiment [33][34][35][36]. By applying large language models to financial sentiment [37][38][39][40][41][42][43][44][45], we extend methodological approaches in sentiment analysis [46][47][48][49][50][51][52] to the cryptocurrency domain [53][54][55][56][57][58][59]. Results show that incorporating sentiment enhances priceonly models [60][61][62], though gains remain limited as Discord sentiment reflects platform-specific user experience rather than macro-market conditions. Future work should integrate additional data sources [63], improve domain-specific modeling, and consider scalability and security aspects [1]. 5Table II outlines the Discord message schema.
